profile.title: Shift-Work Eating Pattern and Dyslipidemia in a 56-Year-Old Warehouse Supervisor Referred for Weight Management Counseling
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment for a shift-worker with obesity (BMI 30.3) and marked LDL/total cholesterol elevation, emphasizing a full 24-hour recall, non-judgmental motivational interviewing in a contemplation-stage patient, and low-literacy nutrition education. The core teaching point is uncovering a patient-vs-chart mismatch: Kasey never discloses his daily homemade 'metabolism tea' or intermittent cinnamon capsule use to any provider (the record shows no supplements), and this hidden information only emerges if the learner asks broadly about teas/home remedies, not just medications. Dental history and old normal CBC values are included as clinical red herrings to test the learner's ability to prioritize the actual nutrition diagnosis.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Millburn, New Jersey, sitting at his kitchen table during a break between shifts

patient.name: Kasey Haley
patient.occupation: Warehouse shift supervisor at a regional distribution center
patient.appearance: Appears mildly overweight with central adiposity. On camera he's in a company polo, sitting in a cluttered kitchen with a soda can visible on the counter. He fidgets, avoids sustained eye contact when weight comes up, and shifts in his seat; he seems a little winded when he first sits down after walking in from the garage.

persona.personality: Warm, polite almost to a fault, and quick to apologize before being asked anything, as if bracing for criticism; uses self-deprecating humor and jokes to deflect when conversation gets close to uncomfortable topics
persona.communicationStyle: Talks in plain, everyday language with no clinical jargon; often pivots to talk about his kids' sports or his church group when a question feels too close to home; needs explicit reassurance before opening up about sensitive habits
persona.emotionalState: Mix of warmth and low-grade anxiety; worried about being lectured or judged the way he feels he has been before, torn between wanting to feel better and not wanting to give up the foods and routines that feel comforting
persona.background: Kasey has worked at the same regional distribution center for over 15 years and recently moved into a supervisor role, which means more irregular, rotating hours than before. He's married with two teenagers who play school sports, and he tries to make it to as many games as he can despite being tired. He's been part of the same church for more than twenty years, where he looks forward to the weekly men's breakfast and the potlucks, and food is a big part of how that community shows love and connects with each other. He grew up in a working-class household where seconds at the table meant you were loved and there was enough to go around, and some of that still shapes how he eats today.
speechExamples: Oh man, don't tell me you're gonna lecture me about the honey buns too, doc already got me on that one.
I mean, I know I should probably eat better, everybody says that, right? *laughs*
Sorry, sorry — I know you just asked me a simple question, I just start talking about my kid's baseball and forget where I was.
It's not that bad, really, it's just... okay, maybe it is kind of that bad.
My aunt's been making that tea for years, it's not like it's some pill from a store or nothing.
concerns: Worried the student will just tell him to 'eat less and move more' without understanding how crazy his shift schedule is
Afraid his cholesterol and weight will turn into something serious like what happened with his dad's heart
Embarrassed about how much fast food and vending machine food he actually eats during his shifts

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment visit. The patient, Kasey Haley, is a 56-year-old warehouse shift supervisor who was referred by his physician after his annual wellness exam flagged obesity and worsening cholesterol numbers. This is his first visit with you. Review his available health record before the call, then conduct a nutrition assessment and counseling conversation.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling after wellness exam showed obesity and elevated cholesterol
scenario.openingLine: Hey, how's it going? So, yeah, my doctor said I should talk to somebody about my weight and my cholesterol numbers — figured I'd better show up before I get in trouble for skipping it! *laughs* Not really sure what you need from me though.
tasks: Take a focused diet and lifestyle history, including a full 24-hour recall of his typical shift-day eating pattern
Review his recent weight trend and lipid panel and explain the findings to him in plain language
Ask about all substances he takes to manage his health, including any teas, home remedies, or supplements, not just prescribed medications
Assess his readiness and barriers to dietary change using a non-judgmental, motivational-interviewing approach
Document your assessment and plan in ADIME format, including a nutrition diagnosis statement

facts.chart: Reports disrupted sleep related to rotating shift schedule.

facts.chart: Body mass index 30+ (obesity) since 2007.

facts.chart: Reports father with history of heart disease and high cholesterol.

facts.chart: Takes no prescription medications.
facts.says: I'm not on any medicines from the doctor, no pills or anything like that.

facts.chart: No known drug or food allergies.
facts.says: No allergies that I know of, never had a reaction to anything.

facts.chart: Reports father had history of heart disease and high cholesterol
facts.says: My dad had heart problems and his cholesterol was bad too. I don't want to end up like him, but here I am I guess, huh?

facts.chart: Married, lives with spouse and two teenage children
facts.says: It's me, my wife, and our two teenagers at home - never a quiet moment, that's for sure.

facts.chart: Warehouse shift supervisor, rotating shifts over 15 years, recently promoted with more irregular hours
facts.says: I've been at the warehouse over fifteen years now, just moved up to supervisor, which sounds great but my hours are all over the place.

facts.chart: Active member of local church for 20+ years; attends weekly men's breakfast and frequent potlucks
facts.says: My church is my rock, honestly. Been going there over twenty years. We've got a men's breakfast every week and potlucks all the time.

facts.chart: Has not discussed his weight or cholesterol numbers with his church community
facts.says: Nah, I haven't really told them about my numbers or any of that. They just see me as the guy who's always good for seconds, you know?

facts.chart: Describes large portions at family gatherings as a cultural sign of love and plenty growing up
facts.says: Where I grew up, if you didn't go back for seconds, people thought something was wrong with you. Food is love, that's just how it is.

facts.says: I bring a cooler to work every shift. Mostly it's just soda in there if I'm being honest, ha.

facts.says: I'm on my feet all shift, so I figure that counts, right? By the time I get home I'm just too wiped to do anything else.

facts.chart: Sleep disrupted by rotating shift schedule; naps during the day and often eats a heavy meal shortly before bed
facts.says: My sleep's a mess with these rotating shifts. I nap when I can and then eat a big dinner right before I crash.

facts.chart: Drinks alcohol rarely, AUDIT-C score 0
facts.says: Alcohol? Nah, that's really not my thing, maybe a sip at a wedding or something.

facts.chart: Never smoked tobacco
facts.says: Never smoked a day in my life.

facts.topic: attitude toward being asked about diet
facts.chart: Reports anticipatory anxiety about being judged or lectured about his eating, referencing past healthcare visits
facts.says: I'm sorry, I know what you're probably gonna say. I feel like every time I come in somewhere, I'm about to get a talking-to.

facts.chart: Admits to sometimes eating an entire bag of chips in the breakroom when very hungry or exhausted
facts.says: Sometimes I'll just... eat a whole bag of chips in the breakroom. I know, I know. I'm just so hungry and tired by that point.

facts.chart: Reports drinking a relative's homemade 'metabolism tea' blend most mornings; has never mentioned this to any provider
facts.says: Okay, there's... there's this tea. My aunt makes it, it's a family thing, supposed to help your metabolism. I drink it most mornings. I never told anybody about it 'cause it's not really medicine, you know?

facts.chart: Reports taking cinnamon capsules recommended by a coworker a few times a week for blood sugar
facts.says: A guy I work with gave me these cinnamon pills, said they help with blood sugar. I take 'em maybe a few times a week.

facts.chart: Reports having privately researched stopping the tea after reading something concerning online, but has not raised it with a provider due to fear
facts.says: Honestly... I looked something up online about that tea and it kind of scared me a little. I've been wondering if I should stop, but I didn't want to ask anybody about it.

facts.topic: what he wants from this visit
facts.chart: Wants to lower his cholesterol numbers without giving up his favorite foods and avoid starting medication if possible
facts.says: I just want my numbers to come down without having to give up everything I like, and if I can stay off medication, even better.

facts.chart: Expresses motivation to have more energy to keep up with his teenage children's activities and milestones
facts.says: My kids are into sports, and I want to be able to keep up with them, not be the dad huffing and puffing on the sidelines.

facts.chart: Believes his weight gain is mainly a normal part of aging that can't be helped much
facts.says: I figure this is just what happens when you get older, right? Can't really fight it too much.

facts.chart: Open to the idea of encouraging healthier dishes at church potlucks once more comfortable discussing his health
facts.says: Maybe down the line I could get the guys to bring something a little healthier to the potluck. I don't know, might be worth a try.

objectives.text: Elicit a complete 24-hour dietary recall from a shift worker, capturing irregular meal timing, fast-food and vending-machine reliance, sugary beverage intake, and late-night eating.
Use non-judgmental, trust-building questioning to uncover undisclosed use of home remedies, teas, and supplements that would not appear on a standard medication list.
Integrate anthropometric trends and lipid panel results into a plain-language explanation of the patient's cardiovascular/metabolic risk.

Assess the patient's stage of readiness to change using a motivational interviewing approach rather than directive advice, and identify barriers and fears tied to his work schedule and social context.

Explore the patient's faith community and family/cultural food traditions as a potential source of support for behavior change, while recognizing he has not yet disclosed his health numbers to that community.
Differentiate clinically relevant findings (obesity, dyslipidemia) from incidental or resolved findings (recurrent gingivitis, prior pharyngitis, normal older CBC) when forming a nutrition diagnosis.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive energy and saturated fat intake related to shift-work eating pattern, reliance on convenience/fast foods, and limited nutrition knowledge, as evidenced by elevated LDL (206.7 mg/dL) and total cholesterol (299.1 mg/dL), BMI 30.3 kg/m2, and self-reported 24-hour diet recall
differential: Excessive energy intake related to irregular shift-work meal timing and vending-machine/fast-food reliance, as evidenced by weight gain of 2.3 kg over the past year and BMI 30.3
Limited food/nutrition-related knowledge related to low health literacy around lipid panels and nutrition labels, as evidenced by patient's own report of not understanding LDL/HDL
Undesirable food choices related to use of unregulated home remedies (metabolism tea, cinnamon capsules) in place of or alongside dietary changes, as evidenced by patient report once disclosed
Not a primary nutrition diagnosis but a tempting distractor: gingival disease — dental history is unrelated to the weight/lipid presentation and should not be coded as the nutrition problem
keyFindings: BMI 30.3 kg/m2 (97.3 kg at 179.2 cm), up 2.3 kg from 95.0 kg one year ago
Total cholesterol 299.1 mg/dL and LDL 206.7 mg/dL, both well above reference range; HDL 65.9 mg/dL and triglycerides 132.6 mg/dL are within normal range
BP 136/84 mmHg, mildly elevated; HR 81, RR 15, all otherwise unremarkable

24-hour recall reveals skipped/delayed breakfast, fast-food lunch, vending-machine snacking, minimal water intake with heavy reliance on sweet tea/soda, and a large late-night dinner after close-of-shift
No prescribed medications; problem list and medication record do not capture any supplement use

Patient initially omits daily use of a homemade 'metabolism tea' and intermittent cinnamon capsule use; this surfaces only through direct, non-judgmental questioning about teas/home remedies/supplements, not just pharmacy medications
Patient is in the contemplation stage of change, torn between wanting improvement and fear of judgment or disrupting work/social routines
Older CBC values (2022) are normal and not clinically relevant to the current nutrition diagnosis
History of recurrent treated gingivitis (2023-2025) is a resolved dental issue, not related to the current nutrition problem
plan: Complete a structured 24-hour diet recall and typical shift-day eating pattern, including beverage intake and breakroom/vending behaviors
Directly and non-judgmentally ask about use of any teas, home remedies, or supplements (not only prescribed medications) to uncover undisclosed intake
Review available anthropometric trend (weight change over the past year) and most recent lipid panel with the patient in plain language
Assess readiness to change using motivational interviewing; avoid prescriptive 'eat less, move more' messaging

Collaboratively identify one or two feasible, low-literacy-friendly changes tied to his existing routine (e.g., swapping one sugary beverage for water on shift, choosing a lower-saturated-fat vending option) rather than a full diet overhaul
Explore the church community (men's breakfast, potlucks) as a potential support for sustainable change rather than a barrier
Document findings and plan using the ADIME format, including the nutrition diagnosis statement and any disclosed supplement use for the referring clinician to review

Advise that any decision about stopping the tea or cinnamon capsules should be discussed with his physician, since dietitians counsel on diet/supplement use but medical safety review is outside this visit's scope
redFlags: LDL 206.7 mg/dL and total cholesterol 299.1 mg/dL are significantly elevated and warrant physician follow-up for possible lipid-lowering therapy
Family history of heart disease (father) combined with his own rising lipids and central adiposity raises cardiovascular risk that should be flagged back to the referring provider

Undisclosed daily supplement/tea use is a patient-safety consideration that should be communicated to the medical team, especially since the patient has quietly wondered about stopping it after reading something concerning online
educationPoints: Explain in plain language what LDL and HDL mean and why his LDL/total cholesterol numbers matter, avoiding jargon
Clarify that occasional treats or Sunday dinners are not the core problem; the pattern of frequent fast food, sugary drinks, and skipped meals during shifts is the main driver to work on
Normalize disclosing supplement/home remedy use to the care team as being about safety and getting better guidance, not about getting in trouble

Offer simple, shift-compatible strategies: packing a quick protein/fiber snack for breaks instead of relying on vending machines, swapping soda/sweet tea for water or an unsweetened option during part of the shift
Reassure him that this is a gradual, collaborative process (consistent with contemplation stage) rather than an all-or-nothing fix
